newsitem.title: USA: Republicans iron out agenda, stress budget.
newsitem.headline: Republicans iron out agenda, stress budget.

text.p: Republican leaders met for the first time Wednesday to work on an agenda they said will focus on "quality of life" issues and will feature tax cuts and a balanced budget.

Continuing in the bipartisan tone sounded by both sides since the November election returned President Clinton to the White House and Republicans to control of Congress, Senate Majority Leader Trent Lott said he saw opportunities for success in balancing the budget this year.

"He's moved in our direction in his rhetoric," Lott said at a breakfast meeting of the U.S. Chamber of Commerce. Relating a phone conversation, the Republican leader said the president jokingly suggested that Lott tell Senate Democratic Leader Tom Daschle that Clinton was switching parties.
"I said, I think that's funny, Mr. President. I don't think Tom would like it. But I told Tom later and he good naturedly laughed, with a grimace I think," Lott said.

Lott, House Speaker Newt Gingrich and other top Republicans discussed the party's priorities for the new legislative session, but on key issues such as the budget and taxes they will wait for the White House to lay down specific proposals before they move.

"I want the president to lead," Lott said. "We have an obligation to the Congress to give him an opportunity to take, as I've said, the first bat. And he has got that opportunity now and he needs to show leadership."
Republicans will prepare ideas for legislation they wnat addressed but will not repeat 1995's storming of Capitol Hill with an ambitious legislative plan for the first 100 days.
"We will not always wait. We will not always react. We will have an agenda," Lott said.

The Senate's version will be formally announced Jan. 21, one day after Clinton's second inauguration. Senate Republicans are holding a two-day retreat this week to decide the first 10 items on their legislative schedule.

At the start of the meeting Lott said they were looking at proposals on "what we can do this year to advance, to improve the quality of life for Americans." He called the last Congress the "reform Congress" and said this year's will focus on "quality of life" issues such as more take-home pay, compensatory time off in lieu of overtime pay and tax relief for families.

First on the Republican list will likely be an amendment to the Constitution to require a balanced federal budget, the Republican leaders said. It failed by one vote last time, but the November election sent more supporters to the Senate.

Other items being considered include more relief for business from federal regulation, highway construction, revision of the Superfund toxic waste clean-up laws, campaign finance and general changes in campaign laws, and legislation dealing with crime and drugs, including a death penalty for drug kingpins and revising laws dealing with juvenile criminals..
Lott also said there might be another vote on a bill that failed last year to ban a late-term abortion procedure that opponents call partial birth abortion.
"We have 18-25 items and we will decide on the top 10," he said.

Tax relief, which could expand to a long-term look at major income tax changes, will be included as part of the 1998 budget discussions and may offer aid for families, a capital gains cut and reduced inheritance taxes, he said.
Lott told reporters the tax bill should be worth more than $150 billion in reduced taxes through 2002, depending on how much money is left once the budget is balanced.

In his speech to the business leaders, he stressed that he felt Clinton was receptive to more relief on taxes paid on successful investments. "He has indicated that he'd be willing to entertain doing more in the capital gains tax-rate cut area than he has called for, which is basically only the home-mortgage area," he said.
